source.title: From Packets to Patterns: Interpreting Encrypted Network Traffic as Longitudinal Behavioral Signals
source.authors: Rameen Mahmood; O. El Shahawy; Souptik Barua; Z. Beattie; Jeffrey Kaye; X. Xu; Chao-Yi Wu; D. Huang

record.tranche_reason: The study applies an SAE to transformer representations and reports results on the interpretability and sensitivity of its extracted features, bearing on V5. It does not test superposition or the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition but reports no test of feature overlap, orthogonality, capacity pressure, or polysemanticity. Transformer probing results and well-being associations are not evidence for the superposition versions. SAE feature counts, sensitivity analyses, and the feature-label perturbation test bear on V5; reported outcome associations are not rows for that version.
record.test_reason: The paper uses a TopK SAE as an interpretability tool on a small transformer trained on hourly network-traffic features. It reports only its own pipeline's outputs: feature counts, downstream well-being associations, label-threshold robustness and a label perturbation check. It does not test superposition, polysemanticity, or whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units. The subject is a 2-layer, 64-d behavioral time-series model, not an LLM.
record.authors_conclusion: The authors conclude that encrypted smartphone network traffic, modeled with a transformer and per-user adapters and decomposed by an SAE, supports interpretable longitudinal behavioral sensing. Stress tracks between-person differences, loneliness within-person variation, and sleep disturbance both. Hand-crafted traffic features capture no within-person effects. They describe the SAE results as robust to mid-range k and labeling thresholds. They make no claims about superposition or about SAE features as canonical units.
record.recipe_differences: The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition but does not reproduce its toy-network method. It uses a transformer over hourly network-traffic features followed by a TopK SAE to interpret behavioral patterns.
record.method_sensitivity: SAE TopK k changes the number and fragmentation of recovered features; high/low label cutoffs cause some assignments to shift between labeled and neutral.

fits_no_version.finding: Across TopK k in {4,8,16,32,64}, the authors describe higher-k SAEs as fragmenting behavioral concepts across multiple latents. The evidence is only a drop in robust downstream associations (14 at k=16 vs 5 and 4 at k=32 and 64).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE decompositions of small non-language models vary with the sparsity parameter, so the interpretable units recovered depend on k (a feature-splitting style observation).

record.peer_reviewed: Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Technol., Vol. 10, No. 4, Article 246 (December 2026)
record.problems: The cohort is small and homogeneous (25 analyzed participants, 7 weeks), and feature interpretation is indirect, based on network metadata, foreground applications, and time-of-day patterns. The paper states that activity cannot be cleanly distinguished from background traffic and that alternative application groupings could yield different interpretations. The tested results do not address SAE feature completeness or canonicality.

untested.parts: No toy-model analysis of overlap, orthogonality, sparsity transition or geometry.
No analysis of capacity competition or polysemanticity.
No LLM is studied. The SAE is applied to a tiny behavioral transformer as a tool. The authors only assert, citing prior work, that the latents are 'dense and entangled'.
No test of completeness, cross-seed or cross-size stability, or canonicality of SAE features.

record.verdict_notes: The record over-reads tool-validation results as tests of V5. The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition only to motivate using an SAE on 'entangled' latents. The adapter 'nearly orthogonal' result (mean cosine 0.02) concerns per-user adapter deltas, not superposition. Recommend reclassifying as T4 with no verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transition, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition or importance-dependent dedicated dimensions versus sharing.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.
Whether LLM features spread across neurons or sparse features in LLM activations can be recovered by a dictionary.

The study evaluates interpretation and sensitivity of SAE features in its behavioral transformer representations. It does not establish completeness, canonicality, uniqueness, or capture of all information in the model representation.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: shared transformer backbone
rows.stage_stated: backbone trained for 30 epochs; SAE trained for 500 epochs
rows.operation_detail: Applied a TopK SAE to latent vectors and counted active and filtered features.
rows.measure: Number of active SAE features and features remaining after the cross-user generality filter
rows.value: 337 active features; 70 remained after the cross-user generality filter
rows.note: The reported counts describe selected features, not whether the dictionary is complete or canonical.
rows.check: Pipeline selection counts (337 active of 512, 70 after a cross-user filter). These are selection values from the study's own method, not a measure of SAE features being complete or canonical.

rows.subject: shared transformer backbone
rows.stage_stated: SAE feature-selection and validation pipeline repeated for each k
rows.operation_detail: Varied the SAE TopK activation parameter and reran feature selection and validation.
rows.measure: Active features; user-general features; FDR-significant pairs; robust associations
rows.baseline: Primary configuration k=16: 337 active features, 70 user-general features, 18 FDR-significant pairs, 14 robust associations
rows.value: 217 active features; 53 user-general features; 9 FDR-significant pairs; 4 robust associations
rows.note: The authors characterize this setting as too sparse to isolate behavioral concepts.
rows.check: The k sweep measures how many downstream FDR-significant and robust well-being associations survive, i.e. the study's own method performance. It does not measure feature stability or canonicality across SAEs.

rows.subject: shared transformer backbone
rows.stage_stated: feature labels assigned after SAE training
rows.operation_detail: Swept high and low cutoffs used to assign behavioral labels to features.
rows.measure: Agreement with canonical feature-label assignments and direction of label changes
rows.value: At least 83% of assignments preserved across the grid; median agreement 95%; no category switched directly between high and low
rows.note: Changes were between a labeled state and neutral.
rows.check: This sweeps thresholds of the authors' post-hoc labeling rule, not the SAE. It tests the robustness of the labeling procedure, not of the features as model units.

rows.subject: shared transformer backbone
rows.operation_detail: Increased one feature activation while holding other activations fixed, then decoded the modified vector.
rows.measure: Whether reconstructed behavioral category fractions changed in the direction assigned to each feature label
rows.value: For all retained features, directional effects matched assigned labels
rows.note: This validates the assigned behavioral interpretation under the described perturbation; it does not establish that features are complete or canonical.
rows.check: The perturbation check validates the assigned behavioral labels through the decoder. That is tool validation, with no bearing on completeness, stability or canonicality. No numbers are given.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SAE k=8–16; feature-label cutoff sweep; perturbation validation
reader_labels.reason: Feature-selection results are described as stable at k=8–16, label assignments remain largely consistent across cutoffs, and decoded category changes match labels (r3, r4, r7, r8). This supports interpretability and limited stability, not completeness or canonicality.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The decomposition yields fewer robust associations at k=4 and becomes increasingly fragmented at k≥32 (r2, r5, r6).
